Like this too is what happened to Jaʿfar ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, when the idolaters sent ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs and ʿUmarah ibn al-Walid to the Negus with gifts, wanting the emigrants expelled from Abyssinia. The two came to the great merchants and the notables of the people of Abyssinia and made the expulsion of the emigrants attractive to them, saying: 'These people claim that Jesus is a created servant' — while those people worshipped Jesus besides God and claimed him to be a son of God. That weighed heavily on the emigrants; and when the king summoned them for the disputation and gathered the notables of his people around him, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs rose and spoke, saying: 'These people claim that Jesus is a created servant.' So Jaʿfar ibn Abi Talib came forward and set out for them the creed of the Muslims concerning Jesus, and recited the verses God had sent down about that: { Indeed the likeness of Jesus with God is as the likeness of Adam: He created him from dust, then said to him 'Be', and he was } (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:59); and he made clear that he is the servant of God and His messenger, and His word which He conveyed to Mary, and a spirit from Him. The Negus then took a stick and said: 'By Him whom the Negus swears by, Jesus did not exceed this by so much as the measure of this stick.' So the Negus was convinced by that and accepted Islam, and his Islam was good; and the delegation of the idolaters returned disappointed.

## Deficiency and Falling Short in the Matter of Creed Leads to Neglect in Many Matters

On the other side likewise: if falling short occurs in the matter of creed, and deficiency in it, that too leads to neglect in many of the matters upon which the affair of this religion is built. We must know that neglect in this respect requires that a person accept a non-Muslim as among the Muslims; that he turn a blind eye to plain disbelief; that he turn a blind eye to transgression against the limits set by God; that he turn a blind eye to manifest innovation, which is a demolishing of the religion; that he abandon one of the pillars of the religion, namely enjoining right and forbidding wrong; and that he abandon what God has taken a covenant from us to uphold, namely the establishing of equity and justice in the earth. This is what God has emphasised in His Book, for He said: { You who believe, be upholders of equity, witnesses for God } (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:135); and He, exalted, said: { You who believe, be upholders for God, witnesses in equity } (Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:8). Hence those who want concession, favouritism and indulgence must arrive at a departing and a deviating from the highroad altogether. This religion is a religion of discrimination, distinguishing between truth and falsehood; truth can never be clothed in falsehood within it, for the clothing of truth in falsehood is the very substance of trial. Al-Rabiʿ ibn Abi al-Huqayq said:

*When the promptings of caprice lean one way, and the listener falls silent before the speaker, and the people wrestle with one another with their wits, we give judgement by a judgement that is just and decisive. We do not make falsehood into truth, nor do we plaster falsehood over the truth to screen it. We fear that our judgements should be found foolish, and that we should then pass our days in obscurity among the obscure.*

## The Danger of Indulgence and Favouritism at the Expense of the Religion
It is therefore not permissible for a person to reach the point of overstepping in his currying favour with people. Less than that was put to the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, and he did not accept it. When the idolaters proposed to him that he keep silent about reviling their gods, he did not do so at first, until there was sent down to him in that matter only the provisional command: { And do not revile those whom they call upon besides God, lest they revile God in enmity without knowledge } (Sūrat al-Anʿām 6:108). And when they proposed to him that he worship their gods and they worship his God, God the Exalted sent down: { Say: You who disbelieve * I do not worship what you worship * nor do you worship what I worship * nor will I be a worshipper of what you have worshipped * nor will you be worshippers of what I worship * You have your religion and I have mine } (Sūrat al-Kāfirūn 109:1–6). So they knew that it was a complete parting of the ways, and that after it no inclining and no leaning towards them could occur. God the Exalted has said: { And do not lean towards those who do wrong, lest the Fire touch you } (Sūrat Hūd 11:113); and He, exalted, said: { And they were near to luring you away from what We revealed to you, so that you would invent against Us something other than it, and then they would have taken you as a friend * And had We not made you firm, you were near to inclining towards them a little * Then We would have made you taste double in life and double in death, and then you would find for yourself no helper against Us } (Sūrat al-Isrāʾ 17:73–75).

The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, then raised his Companions upon this way. Here is Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas: his mother pressed him — and she was the dearest of people to him and the most trusted by him — and she refused food, until she was near to death. Saʿd came to her and whispered in her ear, saying: 'Mother, if you had a hundred souls, and they went out one after another, on condition that I turn back from anything of my religion, I would not turn back. So live, or die.'

We must therefore know that the chain of retreat and indulgence will bring people to what is known today as 'interfaith', that is, the global religion: a disfigured religion combining all religions and all ideologies. It began in the United States of America, and its proponents wanted — first — to combine the three revealed religions, and to take the matters agreed upon between Muslims, Jews and Christians and make of that a single unified religion. This is what does not please God, glorified and exalted, and it is the utmost in alteration and substitution.

Like this is what has occurred among some Muslims too, of seeking to curry favour with the people of innovation, to the point that they wanted to make a fifth school for the Muslims, agreed upon, namely the Jaʿfari school. A conference was convened for that at al-Azhar to please the Shia, and they wanted to speak of the five schools, and to place alongside the followed Sunni juristic schools a fifth school, the Jaʿfari school, purely out of politics and to please the Rafidi Shia (al-Rawāfiḍ). This can never be sound in any circumstance, nor can the Muslims endorse it or be content with it. The colonisers before this attempted much by way of impugning the religion and of trying to make it retreat, and the Muslims did not answer them; and those who answer propaganda of this sort will surely be left behind by history in its wake.

For this reason Sheikh Mustafa al-Sibaʿi, God have mercy on him — and he was in an environment full of Shia and of kinds of people of innovation — said: 'At the beginning of the matter, in Syria and Lebanon, I attempted the call to rapprochement between the people of the sunnah and the Shia, until it became clear to me that I was striking cold iron, and that this matter could never be sound in any circumstance; for they did not agree with me on anything but that they then broke it.' So he knew that this was among the impossibilities and that it could not come about; and for this reason he mentioned in his book *The Sunnah and Its Place in Islamic Legislation* that whoever wishes to strive for rapprochement must make his effort one of bringing the people of innovation nearer to the straight path, not of bringing the straight path nearer to the people of innovation, for the straight path is fixed in its place. There is therefore no objection to our calling the people of innovation to leave the innovations they hold to, and bringing them nearer to the straight path; but it is impossible that we should attempt to bring the straight path nearer to them and shift it from its place. This is in the matter of creed.

## The Obligation of Giving Every Rightholder His Right

As for the matter of worship, it is likewise known that God, glorified and exalted, has given the created being rights: his eye has a right, his guest has a right, his family has a right, his worldly work has a right, his creditors have a right, his offspring have a right, his neighbours have a right, and his calling people to Islam (daʿwah) has a right. These rights must be discharged; and part of discharging God's right is to be eager to discharge every right that God has ordained. Those who are heedless of this, or forget it, are in effect setting up servants as rivals to God, for they suppose those rights to be a rival to God's right. This is the utmost deviation, because those rights were ordained only by God's ordaining.

It is part of God's right over you that you sleep when your body needs sleep; it is part of God's right over you that you eat when your body needs food; and it is part of God's right over you that you drink when your body needs drink. For this reason the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, objected in the strongest terms to the man who was standing in the sun and not taking shade, and made clear that this was severe excess, and that whoever turns away from his sunnah is not of him. He likewise objected to the three men, one of whom said: 'As for me, I fast and do not break my fast'; and another said: 'As for me, I stand in prayer and do not sleep'; and the third said: 'As for me, I do not marry women.' The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, became severely angry, until the anger was visible in his face, and he said: 'As for me, I fast and I break my fast, and I stand in prayer and I sleep, and I marry women; so whoever turns away from my sunnah is not of me.'

He forbade those who wanted to renounce marriage, among them ʿUthman ibn Mazʿun, may God be pleased with him. He also forbade al-Hawlaʾ bint Tuwayt — she was a woman of Banu Taym ibn Murrah upon whom Abu Bakr used to spend — who used to stand in prayer the whole night and not sleep, and used to fast all the days of the year. She came to visit Aisha, may God be pleased with her, and the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, entered and said: 'Who is this?' She said: 'So-and-so,' mentioning her prayer and her fasting — that is, Aisha was praising her for that. The Messenger of God said: 'Enough! Take on of deeds what you are able for. God does not weary until you weary.' Its meaning is: strive to discharge only such righteous deeds as you are able for, and do not burden yourselves with what you are not able for.

He said to ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, when he was a strong young man who used to fast every day and stand in prayer for most of the night: 'Your eye has a right over you, and your guest has a right over you, and your wife has a right over you; so give every rightholder his right.' He commanded him to fast three days of every month, and he said: 'I am able for more than that.' So he commanded him to fast two days of the week, Monday and Thursday, and he said: 'I am able for more than that.' So he commanded him to fast the fast of David: to fast a day and break his fast a day. When ʿAbdullah grew old and his age weakened him, he said: 'Would that I had taken the dispensation (rukhṣah) of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace.'

And when the twentieth day of Ramadan came, and the Messenger wished to enter his place of seclusion, he saw that the tents in the mosque had become many, and he said: 'What is this?' It was said: 'The Mothers of the Believers are in seclusion.' He said: 'Is it piety that you think they intend by this?'
## Excessive Striving in Worship Is an Evil and an Error

A person must therefore know that excessive striving in discharging God's right, set against the suspending of the rights of human beings, is not part of uprightness upon the sound way, nor is it part of travelling the even middle of the road. It is soundly established from the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, that he saw a man of the Ansar keeping constantly to the mosque, and he asked: 'Who provides for him?' It was said: 'His brother.' So he stated that his brother — who works, and strives, and gathers wealth from what is lawful for him, and spends on this brother of his — is better than he is. This requires that the balanced believer who earns and spends on those whose maintenance is incumbent upon him is better than the one who cuts himself off for worship and so becomes a burden upon others and dependent on them.

From here we must know that if a person wants to go to excess in worship and to overstep the limit, then at that point no one contends roughly with this religion but that it overcomes him; and there must come a time when he grows weak before his body, or before his mind, or before his soul, or before his appetite, or before the illness that befalls him. He must likewise be struck with a despondency from all that comes upon him. For this reason it happened to some of those who entered this door and went to excess in it that a man would suppose his station to be very high, and then, when death came to him, he regretted it with the utmost regret, and there appeared to him from God what he had not reckoned upon.

## Those Who Go to Excess in Worship Are Afflicted with Contempt for the Straight Way

The one who wants excess in worship and to overstep the limit in it must be afflicted with one of several things. Either he holds the straight way in contempt, so that he wants to add to what the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions were upon — and this is the utmost of far-reaching error. Ibn Masʿud therefore said: 'Every act of worship that the Companions of Muhammad, God bless him and grant him peace, did not perform as worship, do not perform as worship; for the first left no ground of speech for the last.' The maxim of the people of the sunnah and the community is: had it been good, they would have got to it before us — which is the reverse of the maxim of the idolaters, for the idolaters say: { Had it been good, they would not have got to it before us } (Sūrat al-Aḥqāf 46:11). Every good is what the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, brought and his Companions acted upon, God's pleasure be upon them, and no one later can bring anything better than what they brought. Malik, God have mercy on him, therefore said: 'The last of this community will not be set right except by that which set right its first.'

## Those Who Go to Excess in Worship Are Afflicted with Innovation

Or he is afflicted with another thing, namely innovation (bidʿah), in that he legislates what God has not permitted, supposing the religion to be deficient and that he is completing it from himself. This one shares with the first in manifest error, because he has claimed that God the Exalted does not know what would round off His religion and complete it, and so he has come to complete it by an exertion of his own. Al-Shatibi, God have mercy on him, mentioned that the gravest wrong in innovations is that the one who commits them supposes that he is completing the religion, and that the religion was deficient before his own exertion, and that he has brought something new by which he completes the religion that Muhammad, God bless him and grant him peace, brought. He is thus claiming that the saying of God the Exalted, { This day I have perfected your religion for you } (Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:3), is not true. We ask God for safety and well-being.

## Those Who Go to Excess in Worship Are Afflicted with Delusion

Or he is afflicted with delusion, in that he goes to excess in worship and supposes himself to have reached a high station; and the devil may make it seem to him that the obligations have been lifted from him, and that it is open to him to fall into reprehensible things and acts of disobedience. He supposes by this that he has reached a station in which he is not harmed by disobedience — as the Jews claimed who said: { The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days } (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:80). This condition is part of travelling their road; and the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, made clear that there must be in this community those who travel their road, for he said: 'You will surely follow the ways of those before you, span by span and cubit by cubit, until if they entered a lizard's hole you would follow them.' They said: 'Messenger of God, the Jews and the Christians?' He said: 'Who else, then?' So the Jews who said { The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days } (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:24) have had their traces followed by those of this community who go to excess in worship, who claim that they have reached a station in which God will not punish them. Indeed, the delusion of some of them reaches a great degree of effrontery, so that one says: 'If God were to cast me into the Fire, it would be extinguished.' We ask God for safety and well-being. This is the utmost deviation and distance from the straight road and from this clear way.

## Those Who Go to Excess in Worship Are Afflicted with the Doctrine of the Unity of Being and with Abandoning Deeds

Indeed, he may be afflicted with another thing, namely that he claims to have reached a station in which the worshipper is united with the One worshipped. This is what they call the unity of being (waḥdat al-wujūd), or the station of indwelling (ḥulūl), or waḥdat al-waḥdah, or union (ittiḥād), or the unity of witnessing (waḥdat al-shuhūd) — all of them technical terms going back to this idea in its origin, even if there are fine distinctions between them. They claim that when a person has come to know, certainty has come to him, and they interpret the saying of God the Exalted, { And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you } (Sūrat al-Ḥijr 15:99), in this way. This is the utmost in error and poor understanding, for certainty is death: 'and worship your Lord until certainty comes to you' means until death comes to you. Those who claim that what is meant by certainty here is a known station that they reach have deviated to the utmost degree, have strayed from the even road, and the devil has led them by their halters to open disbelief. We ask God for safety and well-being.

And the one who goes to excess in worship may also be afflicted with another thing, namely disparagement: the devil makes it seem good to him that all his deeds are unacceptable to God, and that consequently his performing the deed and his leaving it are the same; and from here he will leave off the deed on this ground. Indeed, he may be afflicted with obsessive doubt about sincerity (ikhlāṣ), so that he supposes every deed to be lacking in sincerity, and so goes on repeating the prayer or repeating the ablution — as you see of those afflicted with obsessive doubt, one of whom, when he washes his face, can scarcely finish with it. Those who go to excess in acts of worship are stricken with kinds of affliction; and so it is that those who overstep the legislated limit are stricken with many kinds of affliction of this sort.
## Neglect Is a Cause of an Evil End

On the other side, those who fall short — the people of neglect in worship — are the ones afflicted with inclining to the left of this path. They have forgotten the wisdom for which they were created and forgotten that they were created only to worship God, and so they have been neglectful of His worship and have fallen short in it, entertaining wishful hopes about God and clinging to conjectures. For this reason the devil lures them into falling into acts of disobedience to God, and reminds them only of the verses of promise and the reports of promise, while they forget the threat. Such people leave off, at the beginning, the recommended acts (mandūbāt); then they leave off the sunnah acts; then that brings them to leaving off some of the obligatory acts (wājibāt); then to leaving off the essential elements (arkān); and then to an evil end at death. We ask God for safety and well-being. Every falling short and abandoning of worship is an inducement for a person to take on a deficiency and a falling short in the station above the one from which he has diminished.

## Falling Short in the Sunnah Acts Is a Flaw That Passes Over into the Obligatory

If a person falls short in the regular prayers attached to the obligatory ones, then blemishes must occur in the prayer. What people complain of — the drying up of tears, so that when the Qur'an is recited they do not weep, even though were it recited to the mountains water would burst forth from them, { Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled, splitting apart from the fear of God; and these likenesses We strike for people, that they may reflect } (Sūrat al-Ḥashr 59:21) — its cause is falling short in worship. And what people complain of by way of absence of humility in the prayer, its cause is falling short in the voluntary acts (nawāfil). You know that many people are at rest in the obligatory prayer in a way they are not at rest in the voluntary one; when one of them wants to pray a voluntary prayer he pecks at it and pays it no heed, even as regards facing the direction of prayer, and turning aside, and not levelling the back in bowing, and other such things; and when he wants to perform the obligatory prayer he tries to do it well. But he cannot do the obligatory well so long as his voluntary prayer is like this. The voluntary is the fence of the obligatory, and every blemish in it will reach the obligatory. For this reason the scholars have likened the voluntary prayer — and especially the regular prayers attached to the obligatory ones — to the bark of a branch: if the bark is stripped off, the branch withers. (Al-liḥāʾ is the bark.)

Those who fall short in the worship of God, glorified and exalted, cannot be among His friends, because His friends are those who find intimacy with Him, glorified and exalted; they do not grieve when people grieve, and when afflictions come they know that they are from God and that they were written before they came to be, and so they are content with what God has decreed. And when ease and prosperity come, they are not deluded by that, because they know that it was written and has an appointed term: { No affliction befalls in the earth or in yourselves but that it is in a Book before We bring it into being — that is easy for God — so that you may not grieve over what has escaped you, nor exult at what He has given you } (Sūrat al-Ḥadīd 57:22–23).

## Falling Short in Worship Is a Coarseness of Nature and a Harshness

Those who fall short in worship cannot taste the savour of the particular service of the Almighty, glorified and exalted, nor can they feel the blessing of belonging to Him, glorified and exalted. For this reason there must be found in them a great deal of harshness, coarseness of nature, poor conduct and poor courtesy towards God, glorified and exalted, and towards His Messenger and His Sharia. They do not honour the Qur'an, they do not value the sunnah, and they do not honour the symbols of God nor magnify them: { That; and whoever magnifies the symbols of God, that is from the God-consciousness of hearts } (Sūrat al-Ḥajj 22:32). For this reason they do not love people with love for God's sake; if they see one who worships God, glorified and exalted, and loves Him and calls to Him, they do not love him and find no love for him in themselves, because the affective side in dealing with God has been broken in them, and so they do not know love for God's sake. Love for God's sake comes only from uprightness upon the way and from keeping to His worship. If you know that you are falling short in discharging the right of God that He deserves by way of worship, you will love Gabriel and Michael, because they worship God with the worship He deserves; and you will love every worshipper of God, because he is discharging the right that you yourself would love to discharge and are unable to.

Likewise, those who fall short in worship are stricken with other diseases, the gravest of which is boldness towards disobedience. For the worshipper of God, glorified and exalted, is restrained by his worship from disobedience. God the Exalted said: { Indeed the prayer restrains from indecency and wrong, and the remembrance of God is greater, and God knows what you do } (Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt 29:45). The one who does not find this wall between himself and disobedience is under one blanket with disobedience, finding himself together with it at all times; whereas the one who is in worship has a mighty wall between himself and disobedience, and from here his limbs are not led into disobedience and do not persist in it, even if the devil should cause him to slip into it, as He, exalted, said: { Indeed those who are God-conscious, when a visitation from the devil touches them, remember, and then they see clearly } (Sūrat al-Aʿrāf 7:201).

## Falling Short in Worship Is Contentment with the Inferior and Baseness of Aspiration

Likewise, falling short in worship requires of a person that his aspiration not be high and that he be content with the lowest of stations. Whoever has high aspiration wants to increase every day — indeed every hour — in nearness to God, and to be among those who compete for the highest ranks of the Garden, and to be among those whose sides shun their beds at the time of sleep, remembering the race, and that God, glorified and exalted, has now opened the competition to His servants. Whomever God does not forsake is among those racing towards Him with acts of obedience in this time in which the doors of worship have been opened, in which the Sovereign, the Requiter, has given leave to those who would confide in Him to confide in Him, and has not closed a door between Himself and them, nor let down a veil before them, nor lowered valleys, nor raised mountain passes; so they race in drawing near to Him: { Those whom they call upon themselves seek the means of approach to their Lord, which of them shall be nearest, and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed the punishment of your Lord is a thing to be feared } (Sūrat al-Isrāʾ 17:57); { Indeed they used to hasten to good deeds and call upon Us in hope and in fear, and they were humble before Us } (Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ 21:90).

The one who falls short in worship in times of ease, when the time of hardship comes, will not be among those whose supplications are answered at that time, because he did not acquaint himself with God in ease: 'Acquaint yourself with God in ease, and He will know you in hardship.' Those who fall short in worship do not become leaders or masters of the believers; and God, glorified and exalted, has directed us to supplicate with this supplication: { And those who say: Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and our offspring comfort of eyes, and make us a leader for the God-conscious } (Sūrat al-Furqān 25:74).

## The Obligation of Keeping to the Middle Way in Worship, Which Is the Prophetic Way

It is necessary, then, to keep to the middle way, in which there is neither excess nor neglect, in the matter of devotion. Let a person know that the best worship is the worship of Muhammad, God bless him and grant him peace; that this worship is varied according to the variety of circumstance; and that it is ordered according to times and seasons. What the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, used to say in the morning, try to say in the morning; what he used to say in the evening, try to say in the evening; what he used to do when he went to his bed, try to do; what he used to do in standing at night in prayer, try to do; what he used to do of the regular prayers attached to the obligatory ones, and what he used to do of acts of worship at home and on a journey — try to perform it. By that you will have kept to the even middle of the road, and you will find nothing that wearies your body, nor anything that wearies your mind, nor anything that wearies your spirit; nor will you be one who falls short. Rather you will be among those who are increased in nearness, who travel at a deliberate pace that arrives at the goal without haste, with all care and unhurriedness.

This is what God and His Messenger love, as the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said to al-Ashajj of ʿAbd al-Qays: 'There are in you two qualities that God and His Messenger love: forbearance and unhurriedness.' So if a person is unhurried in his worship, performing it with truthfulness and sincerity (ikhlāṣ) and with a mind that is present, burdening himself with what he is capable of and able for, and is not among those who want to tear through the distances and cover the road in the swiftest time — those who neither spare a mount nor cover any distance — then by that he will arrive, God the Exalted willing, at the station that is pleasing to God, and will go on increasing and ascending throughout his life. And if he becomes unable to do something, it is written for him in full, just as he used to do it in his health, as the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, made clear: 'God the Exalted says to His angels when the servant falls ill or travels: Look at what My servant used to do in his health and at home, and write it for him.'

God, glorified and exalted, does not weary until you weary; and He has no need of us nor of our worship. We cannot draw near to Him by what He has not legislated for us. The one who can be harmed by you and benefited by you — him you can draw near to by a benefit he did not command you with, and from him you can remove a harm he did not command you to remove. But the One who can be neither benefited nor harmed by you — to Him you cannot draw near except by what He has legislated for you and made clear, and you cannot go beyond that in any circumstance.
## The Obligation of Moderation in Amassing Wealth

Likewise in the matter of dealings, we must know that the greatest cause of division between hearts in transactions is what pertains to wealth. In the amassing of wealth there must be moderation, with neither excess nor neglect. Those who are excessive in amassing it and spend their time gathering it will lose precious times and rare opportunities for acts of worship. The one who spends his whole day occupied with striking bargains in the markets will miss the times when supplication is answered, will miss the time of the descent, will sleep through the times in which the race takes place among the worshippers who race to God — { and for that let those who compete compete } (Sūrat al-Muṭaffifīn 83:26) — will miss the first row on many occasions, will miss the waiting in readiness ('those who go on alone have outstripped the rest'), and will miss much good.

## The Afflictions That Strike Those Who Go to Excess in Amassing This World

The one who goes to excess in amassing wealth and gathering the refuse of this world and being occupied with it is stricken with a number of afflictions. First, that this world grows great in his soul, so that it becomes the greatest of his aims and the limit of his knowledge, and his heart is filled with it even if his hand is empty of it. For those preoccupied with this world are not necessarily wealthy: many of the wealthy have this world in their hands but not in their hearts, and many of the poor do not have this world in their hands but have it in their hearts. What the Sharia warns against, therefore, is the heart's attachment to it, and that a person make it his greatest concern and the sum of his knowledge, and that he become a worshipper of it, so that his service and his striving are for its sake. This is the destroying danger; and it may harm the one who has it with a great harm, bringing him to the point of overstepping and transgression. God the Exalted said: { No indeed, man transgresses, in that he sees himself as self-sufficient } (Sūrat al-ʿAlaq 96:6–7); and He, exalted, said: { And had God expanded provision for His servants, they would have behaved outrageously in the earth; but He sends down in a measure what He wills } (Sūrat al-Shūrā 42:27). Outrage, transgression and overstepping the limit come about precisely through excess in amassing this world.

## Falling Short in Amassing This World Is Not the Prophetic Way, nor Did the Early Generations Do It

On the other side, we must know that falling short in amassing it is a deficiency on the person's part. The one who turns away from it altogether, and does not want to manage any of the affairs of this world nor to earn anything, is outside the sound way and has not travelled the road of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace. The Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace, took to the means and put them to work, and did not abandon them. Had the asceticism that the Sharia praises required the abandoning of the means, and cutting oneself off for worship, and monasticism, the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions would have done it. Since they did not do it — and we find among them the merchants, and we find among them the wealthy who spent in the way of God; and we find the endowments (awqāf) of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, from which thousands of widows and orphans were maintained; and we find that he stored up a year's provision for his household; and we find that he, God bless him and grant him peace, was given by God the land of the Banu al-Nadir as spoils, and stored up some of it for his dependants; and we find that he, God bless him and grant him peace, used to plant palms with his own hand, may my father and mother be his ransom, and used to draw water with his own hand, God bless him and grant him peace, and helped in the planting of the palms of Salman, for which his masters had made a contract of manumission with him; and we see him going to the markets and buying and walking in them, which is what the idolaters found objectionable in him and what God endorsed for him in His Book — and we see his Companions, who are the best of the people of the earth by the testimony of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, for them, and among them are merchants, like Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, who used to support many families and spend on them from the profit of his trade. His capital was four hundred dirhams, and he used to trade with it in cloth — that is, clothing — and oil, and whatever he earned he spent on those he maintained.

We likewise find ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, who was God's merchant on this earth; God blessed him in his transactions, and he spent on many orphans and needy people, and bequeathed a third of his wealth to the remainder of the people of Badr, which was wealth enough for them all. And among them we find al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam, whose investments were in vast lands and large farms, and who left a great deal of wealth, the price of which, divided among his wives, was riches for them. And among them is Abu Talhah al-Ansari, who had a great many farms and owned Bayruhaʾ, the finest farm in Medina, and who used to pray two units of prayer beneath every palm tree. And among them we find Saʿd ibn ʿUbadah ibn Dulaym, who was among the great merchants and the wealthy, who, when they returned from the forenoon prayer, would go to their farms; and when the day had risen high, would go to their trading; and when the time of the sun's decline came, would occupy themselves with the prayer; and when they returned from it, would fulfil the right of their families. They apportioned their times in this way, and nothing of the good escaped them.

Once we know this, we know that the balanced way requires neither excess nor neglect. The one who supposes that asceticism in this world requires of him that he not occupy himself with amassing this world is mistaken and at odds with the sound way; he has merely travelled the road of the Jews and the Christians, who invented a monasticism out of themselves. And the one who supposes that God is not content for His servants to amass this world from what is lawful in it is mistaken, for God the Exalted created for us all that is in the earth and said: { So walk in its tracts and eat of His provision } (Sūrat al-Mulk 67:15); and He made us successors in the earth and said: { Indeed I am placing in the earth a successor } (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:30); and He commanded us to set it right and not to corrupt it after it has been set right. All of this requires of us that we work and that we set this earth right. But along with that, we must know that the setting right is in it, and that amassing it does not require that it be in the hearts; rather it is to be in the hands, in accordance with the way set out above.

## The Afflictions That Strike Those Who Are Neglectful in the Affair of This World

Those who are neglectful in the matter of amassing wealth are stricken with afflictions, the gravest of which is servitude to created beings. For a human being is created disposed to need and poverty: { People, you are the poor in need of God, and God is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy } (Sūrat Fāṭir 35:15). Hence if a person shuns any dealing with this world altogether, and does no work that brings him his maintenance, he is a slave to another; for the one who spends on him has every pressure over him, since he fears him and loves him and may obey him in many situations. For this reason, realising servitude to God requires doing without created beings, and a person's finding himself with no pressure upon him from anyone, so that neither fear nor covetousness turns him away from speaking the truth and from servitude to God, glorified and exalted. By that a person is able to free himself from all besides God; and so long as a person does not do this, he is a follower of another, one of another's dependants, in need of someone to manage his affairs at all times.

Likewise, among the things with which the one who is neglectful in the affairs of this world is afflicted: his soul and his heart often become attached to it, and he is afflicted with love of it without being aware, even if outwardly he puts on an appearance and shows people that he does not love it, while his heart inclines to it. From here we see today the people of the church making a display of cutting themselves off from this world while they are of all people the most given to wallowing in it; indeed, scarcely does a short period pass without their scandals being announced in the media. In the first age, before the sending of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, they used to amass wealth and hoard it, and the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, related stories of that.

Those who cut themselves off — as it appears to people — are often approached by the devil by way of doubts and by way of appetites; and they are often stricken with a weakness of mind that requires the devil to take them for weak, so that he whispers whisperings to them, and one of them imagines visions in his waking state and sees that he saw such-and-such awake and not asleep, when these are daydreams and visions, and weaker than the visions of sleep. The waking visions that happen to a person when he goes hungry, or falls ill, or exhausts himself with ascetic exercises — he sees while awake the like of what he sees in sleep, like one stricken with malarial fever, who in his waking state raves as though he were dreaming while he is awake and not asleep. So too the one who has exhausted himself in acts of worship and has not travelled the even road that the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, brought is stricken with this raving, and sees dreams while awake, and it is made to seem to him that they are true, and that he has seen the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, or Gabriel, or the Preserved Tablet, or other such things — and all of it is from waking dreams, in that when he grew severely weak the devil made that seem so to him. Some of it may be from visions, but they are a weaker degree than the vision of sleep; the vision of sleep is stronger than they are, because in his body and his mind he is stronger than he is when he is weakened in the waking state.

Likewise, the one who goes to excess in cutting himself off from this world is often stricken with neglect of the rights of others. He is neglectful of the rights of his body as regards health care and cleanliness, neglectful of the care of his family, neglectful of discharging his debts and settling the claims against him. He is neglectful in all these matters, while the devil deludes him that what he is upon is correct; and the more his years increase, the further he grows from the clear way and the straight path.
## The Obligation of Moderation in Spending

Another of these aspects pertains to wealth. This religion is a religion of the middle between excess and neglect, and God the Exalted said: { And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor niggardly, but stand between that in a just measure } (Sūrat al-Furqān 25:67). Those who are extravagant are the excessive ones who go too far in spending wealth and put it where the Sharia does not place it, as though it were a property of theirs to dispose of where they wish and how they wish, when in reality it is a trust (amānah) with them from God, glorified and exalted, who has made them successors in it so as to see how they act. For this God disciplined His Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace, upon this upright way, saying: { And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor stretch it out to its full extent } (Sūrat al-Isrāʾ 17:29). A person must be moderate in expenditure, neither extravagant nor falling short; the middle course is the sound way and is balance in this matter.

Those who are excessive in the matter of spending are extravagant and go too far in spending, whether in the affairs of this world or in the affairs of the hereafter, and so overstep the limit with which the Sharia is pleased. In the affairs of the hereafter they spend more than the Lawgiver has determined, intending thereby to go to excess, and so they return to the limit we mentioned regarding excess in worship. For this reason, when the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, heard that Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, may God be pleased with him, had spent the whole harvest of his palms in a single day, he became severely angry with him. And when he heard that a man of the Ansar — who had a debt upon him — had granted deferred manumission to six slaves, then, when the man died, the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, gathered them, rejected this disposal, and drew lots between them, and so freed two and kept four in slavery, and allowed him only the third.

He would often reject dispositions in this matter if there was excess and exaggeration in them. He said to Kaʿb ibn Malik when he gave him the good news that God had accepted his repentance: 'Kaʿb ibn Malik, receive the good news of the best day that has passed over you since your mother bore you.' He said: 'I said: Messenger of God, is it from God or from you? He said: Rather it is from God. I said: Messenger of God, part of the completeness of my repentance is that I should give away all my wealth in the way of God. He said: Keep back some of your wealth for yourself, for that is better for you.'

Likewise, when he came to visit Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas during the Farewell Pilgrimage, and he was ill, he said: 'I said to him: Messenger of God, I am a man of wealth, and none will inherit from me but a single daughter of mine. Shall I give all my wealth in charity in the way of God? He said: No. I said: Shall I give two thirds of it in charity? He said: No. I said: Shall I give a third of it in charity? He said: The third — and the third is much' — and in another narration: 'is a great deal — for you to leave your heirs wealthy is better than for you to leave them destitute, begging from people. I said: Messenger of God, shall I be left behind after my companions? He said: You will not spend any expenditure by which you seek the face of God but that you are rewarded for it, even what you put in your wife's mouth; and it may be that God will benefit some peoples through you and harm others through you.' Saʿd was the last of the ten to die, and he was inherited from by twelve of his own sons.

The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, did not accept excess in spending from those men; whereas on the other side he might accept that from some people, because of his knowledge of the strength of their faith and their uprightness upon the way — as with Abu Bakr, for he gave away all his wealth in the way of God and the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, accepted that from him, because of the faith and contentment God had placed in his heart, and because he was one who earned and knew the affairs of trade as well, and because he would certainly discharge the rights of his dependants and could not possibly wrong them of a right of theirs. For that reason the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, accepted this from him; whereas as for others, the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, would return it to them and not accept this kind of excess from them.

Likewise, the one who goes to excess in extravagance in what pertains to the affairs of this world must be among the squanderers, who are the brothers of the devils, and this kinship is among the worst of kinships. We ask God for safety and well-being. God, glorified and exalted, has made clear the harm of squandering and its grave effect, and has made clear that He, glorified and exalted, does not love the extravagant. For this the learned Muhammad Mawlud ibn Ahmad, God have mercy on him, said:

*Extravagance, extravagance! God the Exalted has forbidden it, and that is enough. And 'He does not love the extravagant' is sufficient to restrain your hand from extravagance.*

It is enough, to restrain your hand from extravagance, that God does not love the extravagant. Extravagance in the affairs of this world requires of a person that this world become his greatest concern and the sum of his knowledge, and that he love it with an intense love, so that he follows its fashions and occupies himself with it to the utmost. The more its firewood increases, the more its flame increases, and a person grows ever more avid for it, and his heart becomes attached to it until he prefers it to the hereafter. We ask God for safety and well-being. God the Exalted said: { Whoever desires the harvest of the hereafter, We increase for him his harvest; and whoever desires the harvest of this world, We give him of it, and he has no share in the hereafter } (Sūrat al-Shūrā 42:20); and He, exalted, said: { Among people is he who says: Our Lord, give us in this world — and he has no portion in the hereafter } (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:200); and He, exalted, said: { Whoever desires the fleeting life, We hasten for him in it what We will, for whom We intend; then We appoint for him Hell, which he will enter, disgraced and rejected * And whoever desires the hereafter and strives for it with the striving due to it, while he is a believer — those, their striving is thanked } (Sūrat al-Isrāʾ 17:18–19).

Likewise, on the other side, falling short in the field of spending requires miserliness, and that a person not discharge the rights that are upon him. The one who withholds his assistance, and eats alone, and beats his slave, is the worst of people, as the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'The worst of people is he who withholds his assistance, and eats alone, and beats his slave.' His saying 'who withholds his assistance' means that he withholds small kindnesses and does not give his good to others, and so does not benefit them from what God has given him. God, glorified and exalted, has commanded us to spend from what He has given us, saying: { Believe in God and His Messenger, and spend from that in which He has made you successors } (Sūrat al-Ḥadīd 57:7). This includes spending on oneself, on one's family, on one's neighbours, spending in the affairs of this world and spending in the affairs of religion; and abandoning it is part of falling short and stinting, both of which are blameworthy in the eyes of the Sharia.

The niggardly, then, fall short of discharging the rights, and are characterised by the trait of miserliness, which is the worst of traits. The one characterised by it and stricken with avarice must be afflicted with a deficiency in faith and its constant regression. For this God the Exalted said: { And whoever is guarded against the avarice of his own soul, those are the successful } (Sūrat al-Ḥashr 59:9). The avaricious man never succeeds. There must therefore be moderation in this way, between excess in spending and between stinting and falling short.
## The Balanced Middle Way in Character

Likewise in the matter of character. Among the important matters is that a person should know that the straight way is this religion of the balanced middle, which requires of a person that he make his character towards people good: that he not be a spineless follower, all of whose affairs are decided for him by another; and that he not be arrogant and coarse, obeying in nothing small or great. The middle course requires of a person that he be positive, not negative, as the poet said:

*By your life, Abu Malik is neither feeble nor weak in his powers, nor a wrangler with a contentious streak who treats his brother as an enemy whenever he restrains him. When you make him your lord, you have made lord a man readily compliant; and whatever you entrust to him, he suffices for it.*

And as another said:

*When the people make for his house, he is intent upon the best that they thought of him, and that is what he does. He pleases you when he is wronged, and satisfies you when he is in the wrong; so everything you load upon him, he bears — a young man cut to the cut of a sword, neither shrunken nor flabby in his breast and his flanks.*

This requires of a person a complete personality: that he not be a spineless imitator in every matter, such that he says, 'I heard people saying something, so I said it'; and that he likewise not be harsh, whom people avoid for fear of his malice, for it has come from the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, that he said: 'The worst of people is he whom people abandon out of fear of his malice.'

A person must therefore be eager for uprightness in character, and not be among those who submit to everyone, so that they accept innovations and accept what is reprehensible and keep silent while witnessing reprehensible things, supposing this to be from good character and modesty. This is a mistake; rather it is from excess in modesty, until a person oversteps the limit. Even if you are young and weak, you are charged by God and a soldier among God's soldiers; and from here you must guard the frontier post you are in charge of, and not let Islam be breached from your side. For this you must be vigilant, and must be one who enjoins right and forbids wrong, whether you are great or small, rich or poor, learned or ignorant. You must uphold the right that is upon you for God, and must look after the religion in what is next to you, and not let anything enter through this frontier post over which you stand; for you are a guard on duty. Let no devil delude you with the claim of modesty, for the modesty that prevents the changing of a wrong, or the enjoining of right, or the asking about a matter of religion, is the blameworthy modesty that is odious in the eyes of the Sharia, as the learned Muhammad Mawlud, God have mercy on him, said:

*As for blameworthy diffidence, it is what prevents the changing of a wrong, or the asking about a matter of religion and the like; and it is what has been counted among the things that destroy.*

For this reason Umm Sulaym, may God be pleased with her, when she asked the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, about a woman who has a wet dream and sees what a man sees, whether a full ritual washing (ghusl) is required of her, said: 'God is not ashamed of the truth' — and she opened her speech with that.

A person must know that being ashamed of the truth is blameworthy and is not part of good and praiseworthy character; and must know that currying favour with people, and going along with them in what they are engaged in, and attending their gatherings even if there is in them what does not please God, and turning a blind eye to that, is not part of praiseworthy character. Rather, praiseworthy character requires of a person that he be patient with people's harm in what pertains to his own person; but he must be angry for God's anger when the sanctities of God are violated. Aisha, may God be pleased with her, said: 'The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, never avenged himself for his own sake, and never became angry for his own sake; he only became angry for God's anger when the sanctities of God were violated.' This is what the believer becomes angry at: he becomes angry when the sanctities of God are violated; whereas as for his own rights, he overlooks them and is forbearing in them. But in the rights of God that is not acceptable.

From here, going to excess in making one's character good and soft, until a person is unable to enjoin any right, or forbid any wrong, or speak any truth, or take any correct stand, and it requires embarrassment at speaking the truth and at rejecting what is wrong — all of this is from blameworthy excess in which there is no good.

On the other side likewise is neglect in character: that a person be harsh, rough and coarse in every matter, even in the matter of God, so that when he enjoins right he comes with roughness and coarseness, and when he forbids wrong he comes with roughness and coarseness, as though he were a king standing over the necks of the servants of God. This type is not pleasing to God either; rather it is from neglect in character. A person must be schooled in the character that God chose for His Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace: { So it was by a mercy from God that you were gentle with them; and had you been rough and hard of heart, they would have dispersed from around you. So pardon them, and ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the matter; and when you have resolved, then rely upon God } (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:159).

Neglect in character requires of a person that his conduct towards his parents be poor, though they are the most trusted of people for him; that his conduct towards his Muslim neighbours be poor, though they have two rights, the right of neighbourliness and the right of Islam; and that his conduct towards the elderly among the Muslims be poor, though the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, made honouring them obligatory, saying: 'My community will not cease to be in good so long as its elder is merciful to its young and its young honour its elder.' It requires poor conduct towards the angels, who witness his rebuking of the young and his transgression against rights; and it requires poor conduct towards the Sovereign, the Requiter, glorified and exalted. A person must remember God's power over him. Here is Abu Masʿud al-Badri, may God be pleased with him, who said: 'I was flogging a slave boy of mine on the road, when there was a voice behind me saying: "Know, Abu Masʿud!" I looked, and it was the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, saying: "Know, Abu Masʿud, that God is more able over you than you are over this boy." I said: "Messenger of God, he is free for the face of God." He said: "Had you not done so, the Fire would have scorched you."'

So neglect in character requires of a person that he become like the beasts, in which there is no good. We ask God for safety and well-being. A person must make his character good, and discipline his soul, and purify it (tazkiyah), and that must be by the sound way and in accordance with the prophetic character.

## The Evil of Combining Excess and Neglect in the Matter of Character
Many people today, in the matter of character, combine excess and neglect. In one respect they are unable to reject what is wrong or to change it, and claim that this is out of modesty; and in the respect of neglect, they will not sit with certain elders — their in-laws, for instance — nor eat with them, and suppose that this is from modesty and good character. Yet this is excess, and the first was neglect. Both are odious in the eyes of the Sharia. Had this been part of honouring elders, the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions would have done it. The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, used to eat with Abu Bakr, Umar, Ali and Uthman, and all of them were his in-laws; and he used to sit with them in their houses. 'He came to Ali and Fatimah while they were in their bed, and said, when they made to rise to him: "Stay where you are." Then he sat between them, and put his back against Fatimah's stomach and his feet against Ali's stomach. Ali said: "And I felt the coldness of his feet on my back."'

This is part of the courtesy of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, and of his character; and no believer can turn away from the character of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, or suppose any character better than his character in any circumstance, for God the Exalted says: { And indeed you are upon a magnificent character } (Sūrat al-Qalam 68:4). It is not possible that we should come with a character out of ourselves that is greater than the character of the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, or better than it. That is among the impossibilities.

So the one who does this sort of thing has combined the two traits, has combined excess and neglect; and this is very widespread. I have come to know that in some settings among us here — regrettably — you find a man who will not pray with his in-law in one mosque, and cannot stand next to him in the row. This is from excess in character and exaggeration in it, and it is not legislated and has no basis whatsoever from the standpoint of the Sharia. Nor does he visit him when he is ill, and he cuts him off completely — while God the Exalted says: { And among His signs is that He created for you, from yourselves, spouses, that you may find rest in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy } (Sūrat al-Rūm 30:21). Where is the affection and the mercy if a person cuts off his wife's family — not drinking with them, nor eating, nor visiting their sick, nor greeting them, and cutting them off entirely? This, then, is not part of the character the Sharia praises; rather it is from odious excess in character.

We must know that this religion, which God has approved for us, enters into all the affairs of our life, and that the straight way within it prevents extremism (taṭarruf). Extremism includes both things: it includes excess and it includes neglect, for both are an extreme, and taṭarruf is derived from ṭaraf, 'extreme': 'and both extremes of the middle course of affairs are blameworthy'. Today it has become common on the tongues of the media to apply 'extremism' to the side of excess only; and that is because those who apply it in the media are all of them from among the neglectful, and so they are all of them extremists, but they want to transfer extremism to the other side only. The reality is that both extremes of the way are extremism. Whoever knows this way that is pleasing to God, glorified and exalted, and knows that it is the creed of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, cannot turn himself away from it, for God the Exalted says: { And who turns away from the creed of Abraham but one who makes a fool of himself? } (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:130).

## The Obligation of Moderation in Dealings with Women

We must therefore bring this way down into all our deeds, and set before it the small particulars of our affairs, our life and our reality. Among the matters that ought to be set before this straight middle way is what pertains to dealings with women and mixing with them. The straight way in this respect is that woman is man's sister; that between them is that cooperation in righteousness and God-consciousness which has been legislated for them; that each of them is charged with obligations, God having forbidden things to each and made things obligatory upon each, and having set limits for each that cannot be overstepped; and that each of them is responsible for looking after this religion and supporting it. Excess, by overstepping this way, is odious; and neglect, by falling short of it, is odious in the eyes of the Sharia. In this matter, in the mixing of women, people combine the two things: excess and neglect.

In the field of excess, we find that some people disdain women and do not respect them as human beings, nor value them with this valuing; and will not consult women nor seek their opinion on matters of religion, even if they are more learned and more sensible than he is — although God commanded them to teach people, saying: { And remember what is recited in your houses of the verses of God and of wisdom } (Sūrat al-Aḥzāb 33:34). And if a woman gives him a legal opinion, he does not trust it. This is nothing but excess in which there is no good, and a neglect of the right of the woman herself.

Like that, on the other side, is neglect in their rights — I mean excess by overstepping the limit in what pertains to dealing with them, such as forbidden mixing, forbidden seclusion, speech that arouses suspicion, and softness of speech; all of which are among what God has forbidden and among the limits that lie outside the even straight way.

We find that some people, in dealing with women, are excessive and go too far, so that a man does not suppose that he has to return the greeting to a woman when she greets him, and supposes that women likewise do not greet men nor answer a sneezer. So he speaks with a woman about worldly matters, but if he sneezes she does not answer him and he does not answer her, and if he greets her she does not return it to him, nor he to her. Thus he leaves off the obligatory matter commanded by the Sharia, which is among the rights of the Sharia and among the rights of Islamic brotherhood, while he plunges into conversation and its byways — indeed, the conversation the two of them are plunging into may be what is not lawful to plunge into in the first place, such as softness of speech and talk that arouses suspicion. They speak in what arouses suspicion, yet neither returns the greeting to the other nor answers him when he sneezes. There is no doubt that this is a combining of excess and neglect.

We find that some people will not go in to women in a house when they want to teach them, and so place a screen, for instance, between themselves and them; or order them to leave the mosque; or do what prevents them from going to lessons; or prevent them from going to lectures. All of this is at odds with the prophetic way, for the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'Do not prevent the handmaids of God from the mosques of God.' He used to teach women and they would sit with him; and they said to him: 'Messenger of God, our brothers among the men have got the better of us in access to you, so appoint for us a day of your own time.' So he appointed Thursday for them.

The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, did not place a barrier between himself and women; rather they used to pray with him in the mosque, and he would say: 'The best of the rows of the men is the first of them and the worst of them is the last of them; and the best of the rows of the women is the last of them and the worst of them is the first of them.' He used to command the men not to depart until the women had departed, and used to command the women not to raise their eyes until the men had sat up from prostration, lest anything of the men's nakedness be uncovered to them. They used to attend the dawn prayer with him, wrapped in their cloaks, unrecognisable in the darkness before daybreak; and they used to attend with him the Eid prayer, the prayer for rain and the Friday prayers. In the report of Umm ʿAtiyyah: 'We were commanded to bring out the young unmarried women, and the menstruating women, and the women kept behind curtains, to witness the good and to swell the numbers of the Muslims.'

The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, used to greet them, and return the greeting to them, and visit them when they were ill; and his Companions used to do that. In *Sahih al-Bukhari*: that Abu Bakr said to Umar after the death of the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace: 'Come, let us visit Umm Ayman, as the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, used to visit her.' When they went in to her she wept, and they said to her: 'Do you not know that what is with God is better for the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, than this world?' She said: 'It is not that I weep because I do not know that what is with God is better for the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, than this world; rather I weep for the cutting off of revelation from heaven.' So she stirred them to weeping, and they wept, and then they rose.

Umar, may God be pleased with him, used to visit the old women of the Ansar and serve them; he used to milk the sheep for an old woman of the Ansar. He went out one night making his rounds, and heard an old woman of the Ansar beating camel hair and saying:

*Upon Muhammad be the blessings of the righteous; may the good and the chosen invoke blessings upon you. You were one who stood long in prayer, weeping in the last hours of the night. Would that I knew — and the ways of death are many — whether the abode will bring me together with my beloved.*

So Umar sat at her door weeping until the dawn broke.

The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, went out one night into an alley among the alleys of Medina and passed by the door of an old woman of the Ansar, and there she was reciting the Qur'an. The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, stopped to listen to her recitation, and she recited the saying of God the Exalted: { Has there come to you the account of the Overwhelming Event? } (Sūrat al-Ghāshiyah 88:1). So the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'Yes, it has come to me; yes, it has come to me,' and he sat down weeping.

We must therefore know that the straight way in mixing with women requires this: neither excess in it nor neglect. We are not able to follow out the particulars of this subject, but a hint suffices the intelligent. It is now known that the straight way is a balanced middle way in all matters, their small ones and their great ones; that excess in every matter is odious in the eyes of the Sharia and that neglect is blameworthy; and that every virtue lies between two vices — and that has been made known by the examples we have mentioned.

We ask God, glorified and exalted, to make what we say and what we hear an argument for us and not against us; to grant us success in what He loves and is pleased with; and to make our deeds sincerely for His noble face. And God bless our Prophet Muhammad and all his family and his Companions.

editorial_review_reasons: Sectarian: the record rejects recognition of the Jaʿfari school and refers to the Twelver Shia as الروافض (al-Rawāfiḍ), a polemical term, and quotes Mustafa al-Sibaʿi to the effect that rapprochement with the Shia is impossible ('striking cold iron'). Read in English out of context this carries clear reputational exposure, and in some jurisdictions sectarian-vilification exposure.

Inter-religious: the record states that 'the people of the church' feign detachment from the world while being the most given to it, and that 'scarcely does a short period pass without their scandals being announced in the media'. This is a pointed claim about Christian clergy and carries reputational and potentially defamation-adjacent exposure in Western jurisdictions.

Slavery: three passages report rulings and incidents involving slaves — the Prophet's rejection of a dying man's deferred manumission of six slaves, drawing lots so that two were freed and four kept in slavery; 'the worst of people is he who withholds his assistance, and eats alone, and beats his slave'; and Abu Masʿud al-Badri flogging his slave boy. These are historical hadith material cited for a point about moderation and about God's power over the powerful, not advocacy, but they read very differently in English on their own.

Gender: a substantial closing section on dealings with and mixing with women. The Sheikh's position here is the expansive one — women must not be barred from mosques, lessons or lectures, must be greeted and answered, may be consulted and may give legal opinions even where more learned than the man asking — but the section also asserts the impermissibility of 'forbidden mixing' and quotes the hadith on the ordering of the women's prayer rows. The combination needs a conscious publication decision rather than a default.
translator_notes: A transcribed lecture (محاضرة مفرغة), not a fatwa: typed 'transcript'. It opens with a one-paragraph abstract that is editorial rather than spoken, then runs as continuous speech under section headings. The headings are part of the published transcript and are carried into the English as headings; they were not spoken as titles.
Qur'anic renderings throughout are interpretive and are not a substitute for the Arabic, per style guide section 4. Verse references follow the source's own numbering.

Lines of verse (nazm) are rendered as prose in italics per style guide section 4 — four passages: two anonymous lines on Abu Malik and on the generous man, and two from the Mauritanian scholar Muhammad Mawlud ibn Ahmad (on extravagance, and on blameworthy diffidence). No rhymed English was attempted.

The five-rulings mapping applies throughout: this is a lecture about acts, not a creedal passage, so the kalām exemption of addendum section 8 does not bite. The one creedal stretch (waḥdat al-wujūd and its cognates) does not use wājib/jāʾiz in the modal sense.
المصلحة is rendered 'public benefit' per the glossary where it is the technical usul term, and 'benefit' where the Sheikh uses it loosely of what is good for a person. Both occur in this text.

التطرف is rendered 'extremism' and the Sheikh's own derivation from طرف ('extreme') is preserved, because his argument turns on it: he holds that both excess and neglect are extremism, and that the media apply the word to only one side.
